#3 "DKIM key below 1024 bits: s512 (512) \u2014 the signature is forgeable and receivers may ignore it."

#3 "RFC 8301 sets 1024 bits as the absolute floor for an RSA DKIM key and recommends 2048. A modulus below that floor can be factored by an attacker with modest resources, and anyone who factors it can sign mail that passes DKIM as your domain \u2014 which also means it passes DMARC, because DMARC accepts a message whose DKIM signature aligns. Some receivers have stopped accepting short keys outright, so the same record can silently fail verification at one provider while passing at another."
#3 "Generate a new 2048-bit key and publish it under a "
#3 " selector, switch your signing service to that selector, and only then remove the old record. Rotating in place breaks every message still in flight that was signed with the old key."

#3 "; A receiver queries s2026._domainkey.example.com for this key\u000a; Publish the new key first, under a new selector:\u000as2026._domainkey    TXT    \"v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0B...\"\u000a\u000a; Switch signing to s2026, wait for mail in flight to clear,\u000a; then delete the old short-key record:\u000as2020._domainkey    TXT    \"v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MFwwDQYJKoZIhvcNAQEB...\""
#3 "DKIM signs with an RSA key at or below 1024 bits while DMARC enforces: sunparse (null), s1024 (1024), s512 (512)."

#3 "A 1024-bit RSA key is below the RFC 8301 minimum and can be factored by a well-resourced attacker, who could then forge signatures that pass your enforced DMARC policy \u2014 the exact outcome enforcement is meant to prevent."
#3 "Rotate the affected selectors to a 2048-bit RSA key (or Ed25519), publish the new public key, and retire the weak selector once mail has moved to it."
#3 "DKIM selector published with an empty key: srevoked \u2014 the selector is revoked and signs nothing."

#3 " tag with an empty value as key revocation: a receiver that finds it treats every signature made with that selector as permanently invalid. That is the correct way to retire a selector. It becomes a problem when the selector is still configured somewhere as a signing key, because the mail goes out signed, the receiver looks up the selector, and the signature fails \u2014 which looks identical to a forgery."

#3 "Confirm nothing still signs with this selector. If the selector is genuinely retired, the revocation record can stay indefinitely or be removed once no mail signed with it is still in flight. If something is still signing with it, publish the real public key or move that service to a live selector."

#3 "; A revocation \u2014 empty p=, deliberately:\u000aold2019._domainkey    TXT    \"v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=\"\u000a\u000a; A live selector, for comparison:\u000as2026._domainkey      TXT    \"v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0B...\""
#3 "DKIM public key does not decode: sedbad, sunparse \u2014 no receiver can verify a signature from this selector."
#3 "The record is present and the selector is found, so the domain looks configured \u2014 but the "

#3 " value is not a key any verifier can read. Much the most common cause is a truncated record: a DNS TXT string is limited to 255 characters, a 2048-bit key is longer than that, and a key pasted into a control panel that does not split it correctly loses its tail. The failure is completely silent. Nothing warns you, the record resolves, and every signature simply fails."

#3 "Re-publish the key, letting your DNS provider split it into multiple quoted strings rather than truncating it. Compare the published value against the key your signing service holds \u2014 they must match character for character, including case, because the value is base64 and case-sensitive."

#3 " means the key applies to every service, and an absent "

#3 "; Malformed \u2014 the tags are present but empty:\u000as2026._domainkey    TXT    \"v=DKIM1; k=rsa; h=; s=; p=MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0B...\"\u000a\u000a; Correct \u2014 either name the values, or leave the tags out:\u000as2026._domainkey    TXT    \"v=DKIM1; k=rsa; h=sha256; s=email; p=MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0B...\"\u000as2027._domainkey    TXT    \"v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0B...\""

#3 "DKIM selectors use different key strengths, from 512 to 2048 bits \u2014 the weakest one sets your real strength."

#3 "An attacker picks which selector to attack, not you. If one selector signs at 1024 bits and another at 2048, the domain's practical DKIM strength is 1024, because forging a signature under the weaker selector produces mail that passes DKIM and DMARC just as convincingly. Different sizes usually mean a rotation that was started and never finished, or a second sending service set up separately from the first."
#3 "Bring the weaker selectors up to the size of the strongest, or retire them if the service behind them no longer sends."
#3 "DKIM key is 1024 bits: s1024 \u2014 valid today, but 2048 is the current recommendation."

#3 "RFC 8301 names 1024 bits as the minimum and 2048 as the recommended size for RSA DKIM keys. A 1024-bit key is not broken and is not being rejected by mainstream receivers \u2014 this is genuinely common, and plenty of large senders still publish one. It is listed here as a rotation to schedule rather than an incident to work, which is why it sits with the suggestions and not with the failures."
#3 "Fold a move to 2048 bits into your next planned key rotation. There is nothing to do urgently. Publish the new key under a new selector, switch signing to it, then retire the old record."

Nothing is lost immediately \u2014 sending servers retry for days before returning a message \u2014 but delivery stops, and it stops for a maintenance window as readily as for a failure. #3 "DMARC is enforcing while SPF or DKIM authentication is not fully in place \u2014 your own mail can be rejected."

With one method missing, the other carries every message alone, so any legitimate mail it does not cover \u2014 a forwarded message, a new sending service, an unsigned path \u2014 fails DMARC outright and is rejected or quarantined under "
#3 ". Enforcement must follow authentication, never lead it."

#3 "Confirm that both SPF and DKIM pass for your legitimate senders \u2014 publishing whichever is not yet in place \u2014 and watch the DMARC aggregate reports until they do, before relying on enforcement."

#3 "This destination published the authorization record correctly, and then used its "

#3 " to override where your reports should go \u2014 which RFC 9990 \u00a74 permits, but only to an address at the same host. This override points somewhere else. The RFC is explicit about the consequence: "

#3 "\"if the confirming record includes a URI whose host is again different than the domain publishing that override, the Mail Receiver generating the report MUST NOT generate a report to either the original or the override URI.\""

#3 " The rule exists to stop a chain of redirections being used to flood a third party. So this is worse than an unauthorized destination: everything looks configured and authorized, and conformant receivers send nothing at all \u2014 to your address or to theirs."
#3 "This is your reporting vendor's record to fix, not yours. Ask them to remove the "
#3 " record, or to point it at an address on their own host. Until then, treat this destination as receiving no reports and check whether you have another "

#3 "; Published by the DESTINATION, in the vendor's own zone \u2014 note that the owner name carries YOUR domain, because that is the name the receiver queries:\u000a\u000a; Broken \u2014 the override names a different host, so nothing is sent:\u000ayourdomain.com._report._dmarc.vendor.example    TXT    \"v=DMARC1; rua=mailto:collector@some-other-host.example;\"\u000a\u000a; Fine \u2014 an override on the vendor's own host:\u000ayourdomain.com._report._dmarc.vendor.example    TXT    \"v=DMARC1; rua=mailto:collector@vendor.example;\"\u000a\u000a; Also fine \u2014 no override at all, reports go to your own rua= address:\u000ayourdomain.com._report._dmarc.vendor.example    TXT    \"v=DMARC1;\""

#3 "With one MX host, any period where that host is unreachable is a period where inbound mail sits in other people's queues. Nothing is lost immediately \u2014 sending servers retry for days before returning a message \u2014 but delivery stops, and it stops for a maintenance window as readily as for a failure. #3 "SPF (Sender Policy Framework) is a DNS record that lists which mail servers are authorized to send email from your domain. Without it, any server in the world can send email claiming to be from you, and receiving mail servers have no way to verify whether it's legitimate."
#3 "Add a TXT record at your domain root listing your authorized mail senders. Start with ~all (softfail) while testing, then tighten to -all once confirmed."

#3 "; For Google Workspace:\u000a@    TXT    \"v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com -all\"\u000a\u000a; For Microsoft 365:\u000a@    TXT    \"v=spf1 include:spf.protection.outlook.com -all\"\u000a\u000a; For a parked/unused domain:\u000a@    TXT    \"v=spf1 -all\""
#3 "The DS record at the parent matches no key your zone publishes \u2014 validating resolvers will refuse this domain."

#3 "The DS record at your parent zone is a fingerprint of one of your DNSKEY records. When they disagree, a validating resolver cannot build the chain and returns a failure instead of your records. That is worse than being unsigned: mail and web traffic break for everyone whose resolver validates, and it looks like an outage rather than a configuration error."

#3 "This is almost always a key rollover that stopped halfway. Either publish the DNSKEY the current DS points at, or update the DS at your registrar to match the key you are signing with now. Do not simply stop signing while the DS is still published \u2014 that leaves the same failure in place."

#3 "No tested DKIM selector was found. No active DKIM key found among 10 tested selectors. Scored as if DKIM is not configured. If you know your DKIM selector, add it to \"Additional DKIM selectors\" and re-run the audit to get credit for it."
#3 "No DMARC record \u2014 domain can be freely spoofed without policy enforcement."

#3 "DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting & Conformance) is a policy that tells receiving mail servers what to do when an email fails SPF or DKIM \u2014 quarantine it, reject it, or let it through. Without a DMARC record, even a perfect SPF + DKIM setup doesn't prevent someone from spoofing your domain in the visible \"From:\" address."
#3 ") to collect reports without blocking mail, then tighten the policy after reviewing the data."

#3 "; Step 1 \u2014 monitoring only (safe starting point):\u000a_dmarc    TXT    \"v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com;\"\u000a\u000a; Step 2 \u2014 quarantine (mark failing mail as spam):\u000a_dmarc    TXT    \"v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com;\"\u000a\u000a; Step 3 \u2014 reject (block failing mail entirely):\u000a_dmarc    TXT    \"v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com;\""
#3 "No reporting is configured \u2014 neither DMARC rua nor TLS-RPT \u2014 so authentication and delivery failures are invisible to you."

#3 " destination you never see who is sending mail as your domain or whether authentication passes; without TLS-RPT you never see TLS delivery failures. Reporting is how a configuration is proven correct rather than assumed to be."
#3 " address, and a TLS-RPT record if you run a transport policy, so failures reach a mailbox you monitor."
<button class="showme-btn" data-close-label="Show less" data-open-label="Show 3 more" type="button">
#3 "Only one MX host is published: mail.other.test \u2014 mail queues at the sender while it is unreachable."

#3 "With one MX host, any period where that host is unreachable is a period where inbound mail sits in other people's queues. Nothing is lost immediately \u2014 sending servers retry for days before returning a message \u2014 but delivery stops, and it stops for a maintenance window as readily as for a failure. Many hosted mail providers publish several MX hosts precisely to avoid this; a single one is more often a self-hosted setup or a provider entry that was only half-copied."
#3 "Publish a second MX host at a higher preference number if your mail platform offers one. If your provider gave you several hostnames, check that all of them made it into DNS."
#3 "No MX host has an IPv6 address \u2014 IPv6-only senders cannot reach your mail."

#3 "A sending server on an IPv6-only network reaches an IPv4-only mail host through whatever translation its operator provides, or not at all. This is not a security finding and it is not urgent: IPv4 mail delivery is not going away. It is a reachability note, and it also affects reputation, because some large receivers treat dual-stack availability as a signal of a well-maintained mail system."

#3 "Add AAAA records for your MX hosts once the hosts themselves accept mail over IPv6. Publishing an AAAA record for a host that is not actually listening on IPv6 is worse than having none \u2014 senders will try it first and fail."
#3 "Your DS record uses a deprecated digest type: SHA-1."

#3 "The DS record identifies your key by a hash of it. SHA-1 is still accepted for validating delegations that already exist, but it must not be used for new ones, and GOST R 34.11-94 is deprecated outright. This does not break anything today."

#3 "Ask your registrar to replace the DS record with a SHA-256 one. Your DNS provider can generate it from the key you already have, so no key rollover is needed \u2014 only the DS at the parent changes."
#3 "The DS record at the parent matches no key your zone publishes \u2014 validating resolvers will refuse this domain."

#3 "Published, not proven active \u2014 DANE protects a connection only when the TLSA record is carried by a validated DNSSEC chain. Each mail host below reports whether the resolver authenticated its own answer."
<span class="adv-dot dot-miss" data-tip="Not configured \u2014 display your logo in Gmail & Apple Mail">

#3 "MX host resolves only into unreachable address space: dual.mx.test, v4only.mx.test (198.51.100.20 (documentation), 2001:db8::20 (documentation), 198.51.100.21 (documentation)) \u2014 no sending server on the internet can deliver to it."

#3 "An MX record names the host that accepts your mail, and that host has to be reachable from the public internet for anyone to deliver to it. This one resolves, so it does not look broken in any tool that only checks whether the name has an address record \u2014 but every address it returns is special-purpose space that is not globally routed: loopback, a private range, link-local, carrier-shared, documentation or reserved. A sending server that selects this host has an address it cannot route to. It will queue the message, retry for days, and return it. If this is your only MX host you are receiving no mail at all, and have not been since the record was published.\u000a\u000aThe usual cause is a zone that was meant to be internal being served to the outside world, or an internal address pasted into a public record. Either way the address also tells anyone who asks how your internal network is numbered."

#3 "Publish the address the host answers on from outside your network. If the mail server genuinely sits behind a translator, the MX must name its public address, not its internal one. If this record was only ever meant for an internal view of the zone, it should not be in the public zone at all."

#3 "; Wrong \u2014 the address is private, and no sender can route to it:\u000amail.example.com.   A      10.0.0.4\u000a\u000a; Right \u2014 a public address the server answers on from outside.\u000a; 203.0.113.10 is an example value only: substitute your own public address.\u000amail.example.com.   A      203.0.113.10"

#3 "No tested DKIM selector was found. No active DKIM key found among 10 tested selectors. Scored as if DKIM is not configured. If you know your DKIM selector, add it to \"Additional DKIM selectors\" and re-run the audit to get credit for it."
#3 "No DMARC record \u2014 domain can be freely spoofed without policy enforcement."

#3 "DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting & Conformance) is a policy that tells receiving mail servers what to do when an email fails SPF or DKIM \u2014 quarantine it, reject it, or let it through. Without a DMARC record, even a perfect SPF + DKIM setup doesn't prevent someone from spoofing your domain in the visible \"From:\" address."
#3 ") to collect reports without blocking mail, then tighten the policy after reviewing the data."

#3 "; Step 1 \u2014 monitoring only (safe starting point):\u000a_dmarc    TXT    \"v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com;\"\u000a\u000a; Step 2 \u2014 quarantine (mark failing mail as spam):\u000a_dmarc    TXT    \"v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com;\"\u000a\u000a; Step 3 \u2014 reject (block failing mail entirely):\u000a_dmarc    TXT    \"v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com;\""
#3 "TLSA published without a validated DNSSEC chain: dual.mx.test \u2014 DANE offers no protection here."

#3 "DANE works by putting the certificate a mail server should present into DNS, and it is only worth anything if that DNS answer cannot be tampered with. Without DNSSEC, anyone able to intercept the lookup can strip the TLSA record \u2014 at which point the sending server sees a host with no DANE policy and delivers anyway \u2014 or replace it with a record matching their own certificate. The record still appears in every diagnostic as if DANE were configured, which is the reason this is worth saying out loud: it looks like protection, and it is not."

#3 "Sign the zone the TLSA record lives in and get the DS record published at its parent. Until that is done, the TLSA record is decoration. If signing the zone is not on the cards, removing the TLSA record is more honest than leaving it there."

#3 "; A sending server queries _25._tcp.mail1.example.com for this record,\u000a; and it must sit in a DNSSEC-signed zone to mean anything:\u000a_25._tcp.mail1.example.com.    TLSA    3 1 1 ( 87D109DD028655D5370B... )"
#3 "TLSA record is malformed: dual.mx.test \u2014 a sending server enforcing DANE may refuse to deliver."

#3 "A TLSA record is a certificate usage, a selector, a matching type and the association data, and the length of that data is fixed by the matching type \u2014 32 bytes for SHA-256, 64 for SHA-512. A record that does not fit cannot be matched against any certificate. Under DANE that is not a soft failure: a sending server that finds a TLSA record it cannot use is required to treat delivery as failed rather than fall back to an unauthenticated connection, so a malformed record can stop mail arriving."
#3 "Regenerate the record from the certificate the mail host actually presents, rather than editing the digest by hand. Check that the matching type matches the digest length you published."
#3 "Some checks could not be completed (MX) \u2014 they are scored as if the record is not published."

#3 "One or more DNS lookups for this domain did not return a usable answer, usually a SERVFAIL or a timeout from the resolver. That can be a genuinely broken nameserver, but it is just as often a transient hiccup that clears within minutes. The rest of the audit completed normally and is accurate. The affected checks are scored as zero, because a grade this tool cannot stand behind is worth less than a grade that is simply strict \u2014 so a failed lookup does cost you points until it is re-run."

#3 "Re-run the audit first \u2014 a transient failure clears on its own and the points come back. If the same checks keep failing, query the affected names directly to see whether your nameservers answer them. A server that returns SERVFAIL instead of NXDOMAIN for names that do not exist will trip this repeatedly."

#3 "; Check whether your nameservers answer a name that should not exist.\u000a; A healthy server returns NXDOMAIN; a broken one returns SERVFAIL:\u000adig +short does-not-exist-test.yourdomain.com\u000a\u000a; Ask your authoritative servers directly, bypassing the resolver:\u000adig @ns1.yourprovider.com www.yourdomain.com A"
#3 "No reporting is configured \u2014 neither DMARC rua nor TLS-RPT \u2014 so authentication and delivery failures are invisible to you."

#3 " destination you never see who is sending mail as your domain or whether authentication passes; without TLS-RPT you never see TLS delivery failures. Reporting is how a configuration is proven correct rather than assumed to be."
#3 " address, and a TLS-RPT record if you run a transport policy, so failures reach a mailbox you monitor."
<button class="showme-btn" data-close-label="Show less" data-open-label="Show 2 more" type="button">
#3 "MX hosts share one address block, 198.51.100.0/24: dual.mx.test, v4only.mx.test \u2014 the redundancy is smaller than it looks."

#3 "Several MX hosts published at different preferences read as redundancy, but if every address sits in the same small block, they very likely share a rack, an uplink and a data centre. The failures that take out one will usually take out all of them, so the second host is protecting against a server fault and not against anything larger. This is normal for a single-site mail platform and worth knowing rather than fixing."
#3 "If the redundancy is meant to survive a site failure, place at least one MX host in a different network. If the second host is only there to cover a server restart, nothing needs to change."
#3 "TLSA is published for 1 of 3 mail hosts \u2014 the hosts without it accept unauthenticated connections."

#3 "A sending server picks an MX host and looks for a TLSA record under that host's name. Where it finds one, the connection is authenticated; where it does not, delivery falls back to ordinary opportunistic TLS, which an attacker on the path can downgrade. So partial coverage means an attacker simply targets the host that has no record. The protection is only as good as its weakest MX host."
